title: The Battle of the Nile
summary: Nelson finds the French fleet moored across Aboukir Bay, doubles its van at sunset and fights all night; by the second morning only two ships of the line are left to escape.

phases.label: Zealous signals the French at anchor
phases.caption: At two in the afternoon the Zealous signals the enemy's fleet at anchor in a bay upon the larboard bow, sixteen sail of the line by her count; Hood makes out thirteen of the line and four frigates, and so does the dispatch. They lie moored in a strong and compact line of battle close in with the shore, its form an obtuse angle, flanked by numerous gun-boats, four frigates, and a battery of guns and mortars on an island in their van. Culloden is seven miles to windward with a prize in tow, and Alexander and Swiftsure a dozen miles to leeward, sent ahead on frigates' duty to look into Alexandria.
phases.notes: Berry and Blanquet both give two o'clock, Mahan 2.45 and Vanguard's journal four o'clock, with the only fix any source offers, the Pharos bearing SSW four or five leagues. Either the journal's clock runs two hours slow or its entry records when the signal was logged; 14:00 is used. The British are placed on that bearing about nine and a half miles WNW of Aboukir Island. The research note's extent is opened out to the north and west, from 31.48 and 29.85 to 31.55 and 29.75, so that Culloden seven miles to windward is inside the plate and clear of the compass rose; the bay itself keeps the note's southern and eastern edges. The French line is constructed from Blanquet's description, heads SE from the island in a line of 1300 fathoms lying NW and SE at 80 fathoms apart, with Guerrier about 2400 yards SE of the island and 1000 yards off the edge of the shoal; the three French markers keep those positions in every phase in which the fleet lies moored. Their heading is 45 throughout: under ADR-0019 a moored line's front is the side the attack came from, and the British ran down the seaward side of this one, so the van keeps 45 even in the phases when Foley's five are inside it. The wind is NNW in every phase, 337.5, fresh through the afternoon and moderate from the moment the action opens at sunset: no source records a shift, and the two forces are an authoring choice inside the enum, not a reading. Zealous's count of sixteen against Hood's thirteen and four is caption matter.

phases.label: The squadron hauls its wind; cables out of the stern ports
phases.caption: The Admiral hauls his wind that instant, recalls Alexander and Swiftsure, and signals his intention to attack the enemy's van and centre as they lie at anchor: first to secure the victory, then to make the most of it. A bower cable of every ship is got out abaft and bent forward so that each may anchor by the stern where she finds her berth, for where there is room for an enemy's ship to swing, Nelson tells his captains, there is room for one of ours to anchor. Brueys gets his top-gallant yards across, then makes the signal that he means to fight where he lies.
phases.notes: Vanguard's journal puts the recall and the cable work at half past two and Blanquet the French preparations at three, while later accounts put Nelson's shortening of sail at four; 15:00 is the middle reading and the one Berry's sequence supports. The squadron is drawn close-hauled on the starboard tack with the royals in, heading 45, which is the board it stood before bearing up, and this is the one phase where the heading is a course rather than the way the guns bear. The track between this phase and the next therefore runs east-south-east while the heading is north-east: that is the resultant of the board to the north-east and the bearing-up about five o'clock, and two snapshots an hour and a half apart cannot separate the two legs. The inshore squadron carries an intent arrow to the head of the French line, the attack Nelson signalled and the only thing in the file that shows the plan before it is executed. The reserve's marker is on Culloden, closing from the north-west, with a detachment arrow to Alexander and Swiftsure standing back up from off Alexandria; that arrow head is nudged a few cables inside the extent's southern edge, since a head exactly on the frame would be clipped to nothing.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 49, the journal extract set into Berry's narrative
references.quote: At 1/2 past 2, recalled the Alexander and Swiftsure. At 1/2 past 2, hauled our wind, unbent the best bower cable, took it out of the stern port and bent it again.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 50
references.quote: His idea, in this disposition of his force was, first to secure the victory, and then to make the most of it according to future circumstances. A bower cable of each Ship was immediately got out abaft, and bent forward.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 50, the same paragraph
references.quote: the Admiral viewed these with the eye of a seaman determined on attack, and it instantly struck his eager and penetrating mind, that where there was room for an Enemy's Ship to swing, there was room for one of ours to anchor.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 67
references.quote: At 3 o'clock, the Admiral not having any doubt but the Ships in sight were the Enemy, he ordered the hammocks to be stowed for Action, and directed the Alert and Railleur Brig, Sloops of War, to reconnoitre the Enemy.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 67, the following paragraph
references.quote: the Admiral got the top-gallant-yards across, but soon after made the signal that he intended engaging the Enemy at anchor

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 50, on the royals

phases.label: Line of battle; Hood sounds round the shoal
phases.caption: The signal is made to form line of battle, and Nelson hails the Zealous to ask whether they are far enough to the eastward to bear up clear of the shoal; Hood, in eleven fathoms and with no chart of the bay, offers to bear away and sound with the lead and carry the Admiral as close as he safely can. He rounds the shoal with the Goliath on his lee bow, and the long column sweeps round to head for the French van. The battery on the island opens, its shells falling ahead of the second ship in the line, and the French brig Alert tries to draw the leaders on to the outer shoal and is ignored.
phases.notes: Mahan puts the signal for line of battle at about half past five and later accounts the hail to Hood at half past five, both of which this phase takes. Blanquet's fifteen minutes past five for a ship running on the reef east-north-east of the island can only be Culloden, whom every British account puts aground after dark; his clock runs half an hour to three quarters of an hour ahead of Berry's all night, and the British first-hand timing is preferred throughout the file. The inshore squadron is placed a mile east of the shoal's north-eastern tail so that the run down to the van clears the tail as Hood's sounding did; the research note's estimate of 30.13 E would carry the tween across it, which is the one thing the approach was steered to avoid. Both British markers keep the easterly heading of the approach and take up the south-westerly run down the line in the next phase. That is a turn of 135 degrees, more than the quarter circle at which schema 2.7 asks for an intermediate phase, and it is authored here rather than split because the shortest arc, which the player tweens, resolves clockwise, through south, which is the way they actually bore up; an intermediate phase would have to earn a caption it has no event for.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 64
references.quote: he asked me if I thought we were far enough to the eastward to bear up clear of this Shoal: I told him I was in eleven fathoms; that I had no chart of the Bay; but if he would allow me, I would bear up and sound with the lead, to which I would be very attentive, and carry him as close as I could with safety: he said he would be obliged to me. I immediately bore away and rounded the Shoal, the Goliath keeping upon my lee-bow.

references.locator: vol. I ch. X, paragraph beginning 'At about half-past five'
references.quote: as the long column swept round to head for the French van, the ships turned their port broadsides to the enemy, and were steering southwesterly when they finally ran down

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 67
references.quote: At five o'clock, the Enemy came to the wind in succession. This manoeuvre convinced us that they intended attacking us that evening.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 67, on the island battery
references.quote: The Battery on the Island opened a fire on the Enemy, and the shells fell ahead of the second Ship in the Line.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 67, on the Alert
references.quote: the English Admiral, without doubt, had experienced Pilots on board, as he did not pay any attention to the Brig's track

references.locator: vol. I ch. X, paragraph beginning 'While Nelson lay thus momentarily disabled'
references.quote: the wind being so scant that they could barely pass to windward of the reef, along whose northwestern edge they were standing

phases.label: Sunset: Goliath rounds Guerrier and anchors inside
phases.caption: The action commences at sunset: Foley takes the Goliath across the Guerrier's bows and, his sheet anchor not dropping the moment he wished it, brings up abreast of the second ship, while Hood cuts away the Zealous's sheet anchor and comes to in the exact berth Foley meant to take. Orion, Theseus and Audacious follow inside, and the whole van is attacked on both sides by ships that range close along the line. Nelson's division is still standing in outside, obliged to take into their bows the whole fire of the French broadsides until they can reach their stations; away to the north-east Culloden strikes on the tail of the shoal and sticks fast.
phases.notes: Berry gives sunset at thirty-one minutes past six and the opening of the action with it; Nelson to Howe has twenty-eight minutes past six, Mahan a little after half past, Southey half after six, and later accounts 18:20 for the first French gun. All fall within a quarter of an hour and 18:30 carries them; Blanquet's half past five is the signal to engage, obeyed only when the British were within pistol-shot, and is not a reading of the first shot. Culloden's grounding is put here, at about dark, on the British accounts rather than on Blanquet's quarter past five, and she is placed on the shoal's north-eastern tail, about 2,200 metres from the island on a bearing of 58 degrees, which answers Berry's tail of a shoal running off from the island and Blanquet's east-north-east of it. Under ADR-0018 she is a detachment that rejoins within the battle at two in the morning, so she costs the reserve nothing: the reserve holds at strength 1 and the research note's 0.75, written before that decision, is not used. From this phase the reserve's marker follows Alexander and Swiftsure, the two ships still able to fight, and Culloden is the arrow; the marker's move to the south-west between half past five and half past six is that change of body, not a ship sailing backwards. Nelson's division keeps a heading of 225 here because it is still under way and that is its course down the line, not the broadside it takes up at anchor in the next phase. The inshore squadron and Nelson's division are drawn about a quarter of a mile either side of the French line where the true distance was nearer three hundred yards, so that inside and outside read at an extent that has to hold the sighting position as well.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 50
references.quote: The action commenced at sun-set, which was at thirty-one minutes past six P.M.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 50, on the leading ships
references.quote: The Goliath and Zealous had the honour to lead inside, and to receive the first fire from the Van ships of the Enemy, as well as from the Batteries and Gun-boats with which their van was strengthened.

I saw immediately he had failed of his intention, cut away the Zealous's sheet-anchor, and came to, in the exact situation Captain Foley meant to have taken.

phases.label: Vanguard anchors outside Spartiate; darkness
phases.caption: The Vanguard anchors first on the outer side of the enemy, within half pistol-shot of Le Spartiate, the third in the line; Minotaur, Defence, Bellerophon and Majestic come up in succession, pass within hail, and take their stations opposite the French, every ship anchoring by the stern so that the British line becomes inverted from van to rear. Guerrier is dismasted in less than twelve minutes and Conquerant and Spartiate almost so within ten minutes more. The Franklin and the Orient open on the outer ships and the Tonnant follows at seven o'clock, while the rear, to leeward and unengaged, looks helplessly on.
phases.notes: Berry gives total darkness at about seven and the dismasting of the first three French ships in the first half hour; later accounts put Vanguard, Minotaur and Defence at anchor by 18:40, and Blanquet has Franklin firing to starboard at a quarter past six and engaged on both sides at three-quarters past. 18:45 is Berry's sequence read against Blanquet's. Nelson's division's marker is placed outside the seam between the van and the centre, where Vanguard lay on Spartiate with Majestic five ships further down; under ADR-0019 its heading is now the way its guns bear, 225, shoreward at the line, while the inshore squadron inside the line bears 45, seaward at the same ships. The two British units therefore point at each other across the French, which is what doubling looked like. The reserve is still a column under sail: Alexander and Swiftsure are drawn passing to windward of the reef's north-western edge, about 780 metres clear of the shoal's axis, which is the only way round it Mahan allows them, the wind being so scant that they could barely pass. Leander and Mutine are with Culloden trying to get her off and are caption matter; the unit's one marker follows the two ships that will fight.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III pp. 50-51
references.quote: The Vanguard anchored the first on the outer side of the Enemy, and was opposed within half pistol-shot to Le Spartiate, the third in the Enemy's Line.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51, the following sentence
references.quote: The Minotaur, Defence, Bellerophon, Majestic, Swiftsure, and Alexander, came up in succession, and passing within hail of the Vanguard, took their respective stations opposed to the Enemy's line. All our Ships anchored by the stern, by which means the British line became inverted from van to rear.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51, on the darkness and the dismasting
references.quote: At about seven o'clock total darkness had come on

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51, on the van
references.quote: The Van ship of the Enemy, Le Guerrier, was dismasted in less than twelve minutes, and, in ten minutes after, the second ship, Le Conquerant, and the third, Le Spartiate, very nearly at the same moment were almost dismasted.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 68
references.quote: At a quarter past 6, the Franklin opened her fire upon the Enemy from the starboard side: at three-quarters past 6, she was engaged on both sides. The L'Orient at the same time began firing her starboard guns, and at 7 o'clock, the Tonnant opened her fire.

references.locator: vol. I ch. X, paragraph beginning 'The two leading French vessels were at'
references.quote: their consorts to leeward looked helplessly on

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 230
references.quote: By attacking the Enemy's van and centre, the wind blowing directly along their Line, I was enabled to throw what force I pleased on a few Ships.

phases.label: Bellerophon drifts out; the stragglers close on L'Orient
phases.caption: The ship engaging L'Orient on the starboard quarter is dismasted and so roughly handled that she cuts her cables and drives out of the line: the Bellerophon, her lights gone overboard, near two hundred of her people killed or wounded, drifting to the lee side of the bay. At that moment the two fresh ships astern steer for the centre, Swiftsure anchoring on L'Orient's starboard bow and Alexander cutting the line astern to bring up on her larboard quarter, while Leander rakes the Franklin from athwart her hawse. Nelson is struck on the head and carried below, and Brueys, thrice wounded and refusing to leave the deck, is cut almost in two by a fourth shot.
phases.notes: Blanquet puts the drift and the arrival of the fresh ships at eight, Berry the taking possession of Aquilon and Souverain Peuple at half past, Mahan the new-comers soon after eight, and later accounts Bellerophon cutting at 20:20; 20:15 holds them together. The French van goes broken here at 0.5: three of its six ships are in British hands and the first two are silenced, while Franklin fights on. Bellerophon never rejoins the squadron, so under ADR-0018 she has left Nelson's division and it drops to 0.8, four ships of five, with a detachment arrow to the lee side of the bay that is carried to the end of the file. The reserve, by contrast, holds at 1 with Culloden aground, because she is afloat again at two in the morning and so never leaves it: the same rule read the two ways round is the clearest thing ADR-0018 does in this file. The reserve's marker moves to the Orient-Franklin seam and takes the heading of a ship firing outward, 45, because two of its three ships lay inside the line there, Alexander on L'Orient's larboard quarter and Leander across the Franklin's bows; Swiftsure alone lay outside, and the caption says so rather than the heading.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 69
references.quote: At 8 o'clock at night, the Ship which was engaging L'Orient, on the starboard quarter, notwithstanding her advantageous position, was dismasted and so roughly treated, that she cut her cables, and drove rather far from the Line

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 69, the following sentence
references.quote: One of them anchored on L'Orient's starboard bow, and the other cut the Line, astern of the L'Orient, and anchored on her larboard quarter.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51, on the Leander
references.quote: most judiciously dropped his anchor athwart hause of Le Franklin, raking her with great success, the shot from the Leander's broadside which passed that Ship all striking L'Orient

references.locator: ch. V, paragraph beginning 'Troubridge, in the CULLODEN, then foremost of'
references.quote: her lights had gone overboard, nearly 200 of her crew were killed or wounded, all her masts and cables had been shot away; and she was drifting out of the line toward the leeside of the bay

references.locator: ch. V, paragraph beginning 'It was soon after nine that the', on Brueys
references.quote: he had received three wounds, yet would not leave his post: a fourth cut him almost in two

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51, on the prizes
references.quote: were taken possession of by the British at half-past eight in the evening

phases.label: Fire seen in L'Orient
phases.caption: At ten minutes after nine a fire is seen on board L'Orient, seeming to come from the after part of the cabin; it soon breaks out upon the poop, where her sides have just been painted and the oil jars and paint buckets are still lying. Berry tells the Admiral, who comes up on deck though suffering severely from his wound, and whose first thought is for the lives in her: he orders every practicable exertion, and the Vanguard's one boat that will still swim is sent away. By the prodigious light of the conflagration the colours of both fleets can be distinguished; the ships to windward hold on, those to leeward for the most part veer or slip their cables, and in the van the fire slackens and soon wholly ceases.
phases.notes: The readings of the fire span forty minutes: Mahan 20:50, Vanguard's journal 20:55, Berry 21:10, Blanquet 21:15, with later accounts between. Berry's is taken, as it is throughout the file for the times he gives to the minute, because he alone was on the flagship's quarterdeck with a watch and reports the whole night in that form. The French van drops to 0.25 on Blanquet's nine o'clock, when the ships in the van slackened their fire and soon after totally ceased: only the Franklin is still firing, and she strikes at half past eleven. The state stays broken, since the fall is a step in what is left fighting and not a change of condition; ADR-0018 puts no floor under broken and no rule against a unit sitting at one state through several strengths. Nothing else moves in this phase. The British markers, the centre and the rear all hold the positions they took at a quarter past eight, and the phase exists because the fire in L'Orient is the event the next hour turns on, not because anybody changed station.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51
references.quote: At ten minutes after nine, a fire was observed on board L'Orient, the French Admiral's Ship, which seemed to proceed from the after part of the cabin.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51, the following sentence
references.quote: This circumstance Captain Berry immediately communicated to the Admiral, who, though suffering severely from his wound, came up upon deck, where the first consideration that struck his mind was concern for the danger of so many lives, to save as many as possible of whom he ordered Captain Berry to make every practicable exertion. A boat, the only one that could swim, was instantly dispatched from the Vanguard.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 69
references.quote: At a quarter past 9 o'clock, L'Orient caught fire in the cabin; it soon afterwards broke out upon the poop.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 69, on the van
references.quote: At 9 o'clock the Ships in the Van slackened their fire, and soon after totally ceased.

references.locator: ch. V, paragraph beginning 'It was soon after nine that the'
references.quote: Her sides had just been painted; and the oil-jars and paint buckets were lying on the poop. By the prodigious light of this conflagration, the situation of the two fleets could now be perceived, the colours of both being clearly distinguishable.

references.locator: vol. I ch. X, paragraph beginning 'These two French ships had already been'

phases.label: L'Orient blows up; the pause
phases.caption: About ten o'clock L'Orient blows up with a most tremendous explosion, and an awful pause and death-like silence of about three minutes follows: the firing ceases on both sides, and the first sound that breaks it is the wreck of her masts and yards, carried to a vast height, falling into the water and on board the surrounding ships. By then the six van ships have surrendered. At a quarter past ten the Tonnant cuts her cable to get clear of the fire and the Heureux and Mercure cut theirs after her, creating such confusion among the ships astern that they fire into each other; the two drive ashore, and Guillaume Tell, Genereux and Timoleon shift their berth and anchor further down, out of gunshot.
phases.notes: The explosion is the widest disagreement in the battle after the sighting: Mahan 21:45, Berry, Vanguard's journal and Southey 22:00, Nelson to Howe 22:05 having burnt seventy minutes, Blanquet 22:45. The majority reading and the British witnesses carry 22:00, and Blanquet's clock is half an hour to three quarters fast here as it is all night. This phase runs at sixty battle-clock seconds to the real second, the slowest rate in the file, so that Berry's three minutes of silence lasts three seconds of playback; the pause is the reason the phase exists and the rate is the only way the file can hold it. The French van is destroyed on Nelson's own count to Howe, the six van ships having surrendered, and carries strength 0. The centre goes broken at 0.25: the Tonnant alone is still fighting, and the marker follows her about a mile to the south-east, ahead of the rear, because the Heureux and the Mercure have driven ashore in the other direction and a single marker cannot be in both places. That the two are aground is said in the caption, which is where ADR-0019 puts a grounding. The rear is still intact but has shifted its berth down the bay out of gunshot, and its position moves with it.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 51
references.quote: The cannonading was partially kept up to leeward of the Centre till about ten o'clock, when L'Orient blew up with a most tremendous explosion. An awful pause and death-like silence for about three minutes ensued.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III pp. 51-52, the following sentence
references.quote: when the wreck of the masts, yards, &c. which had been carried to a vast height, fell down into the water, and on board the surrounding Ships.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 230
references.quote: At five minutes past ten, when L'Orient blew up, having burnt seventy minutes, the six Van ships had surrendered.

references.locator: ch. V, paragraph beginning 'It was soon after nine that the'
references.quote: This tremendous explosion was followed by a silence not less awful: the firing immediately ceased on both sides; and the first sound which broke the silence, was the dash of her shattered masts and yards, falling into the water from the vast height to which they had been exploded.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70
references.quote: At a quarter past 10, the Tonnant cut her cable, to avoid the fire from L'Orient

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70, the following sentences
references.quote: The Heureux and Mercure conceived that they ought likewise to cut their cables. This manoeuvre created so much confusion among the Rear Ships, that they fired into each other

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70, on the rear
references.quote: The Guillaume Tell, Le Genereux, and Le Timoleon, shifted their berth, and anchored further down, out of gun-shot.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52, on the Alexander
references.quote: A port fire from L'Orient fell into the main royal of the Alexander, the fire occasioned by which was, however, extinguished in about two minutes.

phases.label: The fight moves down to the rear
phases.caption: After the pause the firing is renewed with the ships to leeward of the centre, ceases again about twenty minutes past ten for ten minutes, and is then revived and kept up until about three in the morning. Such British ships as are in a condition to move go down upon the fresh ships of the enemy: messages pass from ship to ship, captains consult and propose to move together, and move separately. Towards eleven the Franklin recommences the action with a few of her lower-deck guns and at half past she strikes; the action in the rear grows warm at three quarters past eleven, the dismasted Tonnant cuts her cable a second time at three in the morning, and at half past three the firing ceases throughout the line.
phases.notes: This phase begins at eleven at night on 1 August and holds until five past five the next morning, so it is the phase that carries the file across midnight: it stays on day 0, because ADR-0013 puts the day on the instant the picture is true and not on the interval, and the two phases after it carry day 1. It is also the longest interval in the file, six hours and five minutes, and runs at the fastest rate, nine hundred to one, so it plays in about twenty-four seconds. Berry's three in the morning for the end of the firing is taken over Vanguard's journal at 02:55 and Blanquet's half past three; a claim found in later summaries that the battle was over by midnight is contradicted by every witness on both sides and is not used. The French rear goes engaged from three quarters past eleven on Blanquet's account, the first time it fires all battle. The British markers move a few cables down the line to the ships they went down upon, and the moves are deliberately small: the tween spreads them over six hours, which is what the sources describe, ships warping and towing themselves into new berths through the night with crews that dropped asleep under the capstan bars between hauls.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52
references.quote: After this awful scene, the firing was recommenced with the Ships to leeward of the Centre, till twenty minutes past ten, when there was a total cessation of firing for about ten minutes; after which it was revived till about three in the morning, when it again ceased.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52, the following sentence
references.quote: such British ships as were in a condition to move, had gone down upon the fresh Ships of the Enemy, which occasioned these renewals of the fight

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70
references.quote: Towards 11 o'clock, the Franklin, anxious to preserve the trust confided to her, recommenced the Action with a few of her lower-deck guns

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70, the following sentences
references.quote: The Action in the Rear of the Fleet was very trifling, until three-quarters past 11 o'clock, when it became very warm. Three of the Enemy's Ships were engaging them

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70, on the Tonnant
references.quote: At half-past 3 o'clock the Action ceased throughout the Line.

references.locator: vol. I ch. X, paragraph beginning 'It was therefore perfectly characteristic of Nelson'
references.quote: Messages went from ship to ship, captains consulted together and proposed to move together, and did move separately

phases.label: Daybreak: only two of the enemy have colours flying
phases.caption: At five minutes past five in the morning Le Guillaume Tell and Le Genereux are the only French ships of the line that have their colours flying. At fifty-four minutes past five the frigate L'Artemise fires a broadside and strikes, and her captain then sets her on fire and quits her; at six two British ships join those engaging the rear and open on the Heureux and the Mercure, aground, which strike one after the other. Culloden has been got off the shoal since two in the morning with her rudder beaten away and the Audacious is detached to the Bellerophon's assistance, but the enemy, says Blanquet, had received such damage in their masts and yards that they did not get under way to attack what was left of the French fleet.
phases.notes: Berry's five past five is preferred to the sunrise at four given in later accounts, which is an hour before civil sunrise at this latitude and date. This is the first phase on the second day: it carries day 1, and the caption band's date advances to 2 August with it, which is the whole reason the file needs two entries in dates. The French centre is destroyed here, the Heureux and Mercure taken aground and the Tonnant a dismasted hulk that does not strike until the third; the rear is still engaged though out of gunshot, with its colours flying, and engaged is right for it under ADR-0018 because its cohesion held. Culloden is afloat again, so the reserve carries no detachment arrow from this phase on and stays at strength 1, having lost nothing that did not come back; that is the return ADR-0018 says costs nothing, and it is why the reserve never drops below 1 in eleven phases. The frigates, the gun-boats, the bombs and the brigs are caption matter throughout the file: the roster is six squadrons and carries no frigate unit, so Artemise burning and Serieuse sunk are said in captions and cited, never drawn.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52
references.quote: At five minutes past five in the morning, the two Rear ships of the Enemy, Le Guillaume Tell and Le Genereux, were the only French ships of the Line that had their colours flying.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52, the following sentence
references.quote: At fifty-four minutes past five, a French frigate, L'Artemise, fired a broadside and struck her colours

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70
references.quote: At 6 o'clock, two English Ships joined those which had been engaging the Rear, and began firing on the Heureux and Mercure, which were aground. The former soon struck, and the latter followed

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 70, the following passage
references.quote: The Enemy, without doubt, had received great damage in their masts and yards, as they did not get under weigh to attack the remains of the French Fleet.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52, on the Culloden
references.quote: It was not till the morning of the second, that the Culloden could be got off

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52, on the Audacious
references.quote: The Audacious was in the morning detached to her assistance

phases.label: Villeneuve cuts and stands out to sea
phases.caption: At eleven o'clock Le Genereux and Le Guillaume Tell, with the two frigates La Justice and La Diane, cut their cables and stand out to sea; Hood most handsomely endeavours to prevent them, but there is no other ship in a condition to support the Zealous and she is called in. The division ranges along the British line on opposite tacks within pistol-shot, takes their broadsides, and is still in sight at sunset, while at noon the Timoleon, not in a state to put to sea, steers right for the shore under her foresail and her foremast falls as she strikes the ground. Victory, says Nelson, is not a name strong enough for such a scene: he calls it a conquest.
phases.notes: Berry gives eleven o'clock, Vanguard's journal half past eleven under way with the Zealous firing at a quarter to one, Blanquet three quarters past eleven, Mahan about noon; Berry's is taken. The rear breaks at 0.67: two of its three ships of the line get away and the Timoleon runs ashore, and the detachment arrow to the north-east carries the two that escaped out towards the mouth of the bay while the marker stays where the division formed its line. It is the one French unit in the file that is under way, so it is the one drawn as a column, in file along its course of 45, where the moored squadrons are lines showing the broadside they presented. Zealous's chase and recall is a detachment from the inshore squadron that returns within the battle and so costs it nothing, the same reading of ADR-0018 that leaves Culloden free. The file ends at two o'clock on the second day, when public service was performed on the Vanguard's quarter-deck and the picture stops changing; the coda of the third of August, the Timoleon burnt and the Tonnant struck and drifted ashore, is caption matter here and would need a third day and a third entry in dates to draw.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 52
references.quote: At eleven o'clock, Le Genereux and Guillaume Tell, with the two Frigates, La Justice and La Diane, cut their cables and stood out to sea, pursued by the Zealous, Captain Hood

references.locator: London Gazette 15065 pp. 915-916; Nicolas vol. III p. 57
references.quote: The Ships of the Enemy, all but their Two Rear Ships, are nearly dismasted; and those Two, with Two Frigates, I am sorry to say, made their Escape; nor was it, I assure you, in my Power to prevent them. Captain Hood most handsomely endeavoured to do it, but I had no Ship in a Condition to support the Zealous, and I was obliged to call her in.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 71
references.quote: at three-quarters past 11, Le Guillaume Tell, Le Genereux, La Diane, and La Justice, were under weigh, and formed in Line of Battle

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 71, the following sentences
references.quote: At noon, the Timoleon, which probably was not in a state to put to sea, steered right for the shore, under her foresail, and as soon as she struck the ground, her foremast fell.

references.locator: ch. V, paragraph beginning 'The firing recommenced with the ships to'
references.quote: "Victory," said Nelson, "is not a name strong enough for such a scene:" he called it a conquest.

references.locator: Nicolas vol. III p. 53, on the thanksgiving
references.quote: At two o'clock accordingly on that day, public service was performed on the quarter-deck of the Vanguard
